newsitem.title: USA: June construction spending fell but May revised up.
newsitem.headline: June construction spending fell but May revised up.

text.p: Spending on new construction fell unexpectedly in June, the Commerce Department said on Monday, but from a much stronger level of May building activity than previously estimated.
June construction spending dropped 1.1 percent to a seasonally adjusted annual rate of $591.5 billion -- the biggest monthly falloff in six months, since a 1.2 percent plunge in December last year.

But the June decline followed a sharply revised 0.3 percent gain in May spending to an annual rate of $597.9 billion instead of a 1.8 percent fall to $585 billion as the department estimated a month ago.

The decrease in June spending was concentrated in the private sector, including weaker new-home building. By contrast, public or taxpayer-financed spending on projects like new highways and street repairs increased from May.
The weaker June spending pace was sharply contrary to Wall Street economists' expectations of a 1.1 percent pickup in monthly spending instead of a decline.

Construction spending was exceptionally robust at the beginning of the year, when unusually mild weather in much of the country enabled builders to move forward on housing and other projects. The unusual burst of building in the winter months may have borrowed from activity later in the year.
Nonetheless, the building rate at mid-year was well ahead of the pace a year earlier, with June spending running 4.1 percent higher than the $568.2-billion annual rate posted in June 1996.
Spending on privately financed construction projects in June fell 1.6 percent to $454.8 billion a year after a 1.1 percent increase in May.

Within that category, spending on new homes and apartments was down 1.2 percent to a rate of $256.4 billion following a 0.2 percent decline in May. Spending on single-family homes was down 1.1 percent to a rate of $159.3 billion.

Reduced spending on new housing was a surprise, since the Commerce Department reported in mid-July that starts on new homes had gained 4.8 percent in June to a seasonally adjusted annual rate of 1.45 million.

Government spending on construction projects rose 0.7 percent in June to an annual rate of $136.7 billion after a 2.5 percent drop in May. Spending rose on construction of hospitals and other public buildings as well as on highways and for new water-treatment plants but declined for sewers, schools and conservation projects.
After allowing for inflation, total construction spending fell 1.4 percent in June to a seasonally adjusted $499.3 billion annual rate following a 0.2 percent drop in May, the department said.
